catalog_quote: Some allow contour tones only on long syllables, for example Hausa and many Bantu languages (Tachoni, Dembwa Taita) have just falling tone (F) and only on long syllables. ... In these languages, short syllables can only have level tone. Languages like Tachoni, which limit tones to one-per-mora, are “contourless” in the moraic sense, but from the syllabic perspective, they allow contours. In contrast, Miya has long vowels but no R or F, and Tachoni still has only one of the expected contours on long vowels.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tachoni is described as a tone language (H vs. L per mora, with a falling contour possible only on long vowels); the verbal system has a lexical /H/ vs toneless root contrast plus tense-determined melodic H tones (Ebarb, Green & Marlo 2014 after Odden 2009). No source opened says anything about word stress or accent placement in Tachoni.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal detail second-hand from Odden 2009 via Ebarb et al. 2014: root H deleted before a melodic H (Reverse Meeussen's Rule); object-prefix H shifts to stem-initial syllable (Prefix Hop).
new_statements.domain_note: Odden's remark is about the tone-bearing unit (mora) and contours on long vowels, a general typological aside; the Ebarb et al. data are verb forms (infinitive and future) in isolation. Nothing on phrase-level prominence or penultimate lengthening for Tachoni.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern Tachoni/Lutachoni of Bungoma-Kakamega (Luyia JE31E per Maho 2009 as cited in Osotsi 2020), i.e. tach1242 itself; Odden's Tachoni data (2009, 2020) are the same variety. Kabarasi (Lukabarasi, a neighbouring Luyia variety with its own recent tone description, Marlo et al. 2016 in Language) is a different glottocode and was not used.

tone_statements.quote: This study examined tonal adaptation of Olubukusu and Kiswahili loan words among children acquiring Olutachoni. Olubukusu and Olutachoni are tone languages and tone plays an important role in showing lexical differentiation in minimal pairs and word class. Marlo (2011) identifies three basic tone patterns: Low (L) [↘] High (H) [↗] Down stepped [ ] This study settled on the low (L) [↘] and High (H) [↗] tone as the basic tones in Olutachoni, Olubukusu and Kiswahili. According to Marlo (2011), Olubukusu and Kiswahili nouns are characterized by a rising tone whereas Olutachoni nouns are characterized by a falling tone.

tone_statements.quote: 2.2.0 Tone Generally Tachoni language is tonal; however, the most significant part of the tone in this language is when some words have similar spellings but different pronunciation which brings about different meaning. For example, the word yinjila and halala has two meanings depending on how you pronounce it. Yínjílà ‘come in’ Yínjìlà ‘road’ Hálālā ‘one place’ Hálálà ‘help someone in need’

tone_statements.citation: Odden, David. n.d. Curriculum vitae (14 pp.), linked fromhttps://sites.google.com/view/oddenlinguistics/home
tone_statements.quote: In Tachoni, long penults with H have falling tone (oxutéexa ‘to cook’) and before the penult a long H syllable is level-H (oxutééxela ‘to cook for’). Rising tones always become level H, so underlying /oxu-íra/ undergoes glide formation which should yield oxwiíra, but this surfaces as [oxwííra] ‘to kill’. This gives rise to a limited derivational contrast between level H versus fall on the penult. [...] For example, in Tachoni, the melodic H of the remote future appears from the second stem syllable to the penult with L verb roots, but from the third syllable to the penult with H roots (58a).
tone_statements.locator: author's draft p. 22 (tone-contours paragraph 'In Tachoni, long penults with H have falling tone..') and p. 28 (melodic-tone paragraph 'For example, in Tachoni, the melodic H of the remote future..' with ex. (58) 'Tachoni'); p. 29 carries no Tachoni material
